TASK: Build the **inline 5-stage build wizard**, as a self-contained component another agent will mount on the Create Website page. Today "Help me write it" navigates away to `/wizard`; it must instead open in place.

READ FIRST:
1. `docs/design-system.md` — binding contract.
2. `components/ui/*` — `Modal`, `Field`, `Segmented`, `Badge`, `Button`, `Card`, `AIProgress`. Import them; never hand-roll a second version.
3. `components/wizard/PromptWizard.tsx` (695 lines), `LookPicker.tsx`, `ImportStep.tsx`, and `lib/wizard.ts` — **the existing wizard and its prompt-assembly logic. This is your foundation. Read all of it.** The public `/wizard` page must keep working unchanged.
4. `lib/brand-kit.ts` — colour/brand vocabulary.
5. `lib/templates.ts` — how a good build brief actually reads. The 23 prompts are the quality bar for what your wizard must assemble.
6. `lib/agent.ts` — the SYSTEM prompt. **Read what a generated site actually IS**: one page, no backend, no accounts, no database. This governs which "features" are honestly offerable.
7. `app/api/import/fetcher.ts` — the URL-import gate, and why it is named after the service.

## YOU OWN
`components/wizard/InlineWizard.tsx` (new) and any new files under `components/wizard/`, plus `lib/features.ts` (new). Do NOT edit `PromptWizard.tsx`, `LookPicker.tsx`, `ImportStep.tsx`, `lib/wizard.ts`, `app/wizard/**`, `app/**`, `components/ui/**`, or `components/templates/**` (another agent owns that).

If you need logic out of `PromptWizard.tsx` or `lib/wizard.ts`, **import it if it is exported; copy it into your own file if it is not.** Do not edit theirs.

## THE EXACT INTERFACE — another agent mounts this

```tsx
export type InlineWizardResult = {
  /** The finished, editable build prompt. */
  prompt: string;
  logoDataUrl?: string;
  palette?: string[];
};

export function InlineWizard(props: {
  open: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
  onComplete: (result: InlineWizardResult) => void;
}): React.ReactNode;
```

A stub with this exact signature already exists at that path. Replace it.

## THE FIVE STAGES

1. **Describe** — what are you building, in their own words.
2. **Site details** — name, location, what they do, contact details, hours; whatever the brief genuinely needs.
3. **Style & layout** — colour scheme, mood, typography feel, layout shape. Logo upload here.
4. **Features** — see below.
5. **Review & build** — the assembled prompt, fully editable, with an honest credit estimate (`estimateCredits("create")`, shown as a RANGE not a quote).

Clean and organised, with the **Kodely logo above the wizard** (`components/marketing/Logo.tsx` exports `Logo` and `Mark`). A clear stage indicator. Back and forward without losing answers. Every stage skippable — someone must be able to reach Review from stage 1.

## STAGE 4 AND `lib/features.ts` — THE PART THAT NEEDS JUDGEMENT

Build a **feature library**: a typed catalogue of site features a customer can toggle on, where each feature contributes a precise, well-written fragment to the build prompt. This is foundation work — it should be easy to add features later.

**The hard constraint, and you must respect it:** read `lib/agent.ts` and find out exactly what a generated site can and cannot do. It is a single-page React app with no backend, no database and no accounts. `lib/site-forms.ts` means contact forms on PUBLISHED sites genuinely work and email the owner — verify that yourself and note that draft previews do not have working forms.

So: a booking system with real availability, user logins, e-commerce checkout, and a searchable database are **not honestly offerable**. A contact form, an opening-hours table, a gallery, a pricing table, testimonials, an FAQ accordion, a map embed (check the CSP first — `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts` sets `connect-src 'none'` and a restrictive `img-src`; a third-party map iframe will very likely be blocked, so **verify before offering it**) probably are.

**Categorise every feature you consider as offerable or not, and put the not-offerable ones in your report with the reason.** Do not silently drop them and do not offer them greyed-out with a fake "Pro" lock. If a feature is nearly-offerable, say what would make it real.

Each feature needs: id, label, a one-line customer-facing description that is TRUE, a category, and the prompt fragment. Where a feature has a caveat the customer should know (e.g. "the form works once your site is published, not in preview"), the UI must say it.

## HARD RULES
- **Never build something that only pretends to work.** This applies doubly to the feature list — every toggle is a promise about the finished site.
- Logo upload: follow `app/(portal)/dashboard/new/image.ts` (read it) so output always matches the `data:image/(png|jpeg|webp);base64,` regex the generate route enforces.
- `k-focus` everywhere, works in both themes, focus moves sensibly on stage change, and the stage indicator is announced to assistive tech.
- Must pass `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components --max-warnings=0`, zero errors zero warnings.

REPORT BACK: your feature library and — importantly — the full list of features you REFUSED to offer with the reason for each, what you reused vs copied from the existing wizard, your verdict on map embeds under the real CSP, and anything untested.

1	# Kodely product design system
2	
3	The contract for the customer-facing portal (`app/(portal)/**`) and the builder
4	(`app/projects/[id]/**`). Marketing pages (`app/page.tsx`, `/pricing`, `/blog`,
5	`/templates`, `/wizard`) are a **separate** system — do not repoint their tokens.
6	
7	## The one-sentence brief
8	
9	An AI website builder that happens to have a customer portal around it — not a
10	dashboard that happens to contain a builder. The primary action is always
11	"build something".
12	
13	---
14	
15	## Tokens
16	
17	Defined in `app/globals.css`, exposed to Tailwind via `@theme inline`. **Use the
18	Tailwind class, never a raw hex and never an arbitrary-value bracket.**
19	
20	### Surface
21	
22	| Class | Use |
23	| --- | --- |
24	| `bg-canvas` | The page behind panels. Set by `AppShell`; pages never set it. |
25	| `bg-surface` | Cards, panels, the sidebar. |
26	| `bg-surface-2` | Hover, inset rows, quiet fills. |
27	| `bg-surface-3` | Track of a progress bar, the deepest step. |
28	| `bg-inset` | Code/preview wells. |
29	
30	### Line
31	
32	`border-hair` (default for cards) · `border-line-mid` (inputs, menus) ·
33	`border-line-strong` (emphasis, pending step outline)
34	
35	### Text
36	
37	`text-ink` (primary) · `text-ink-2` (secondary/body) · `text-ink-3` (tertiary,
38	placeholder, disabled) · `text-ink-inv` (on a brand fill)
39	
40	### Brand
41	
42	`text-brand` `bg-brand` `bg-brand-tint` `bg-brand-tint-2` `text-brand-ink`
43	
44	`--brand-gradient` is a **fill of last resort**. Exactly one element per view may
45	carry it: the primary button. Do not gradient headings, cards, borders or icons.
46	
47	### Status
48	
49	`ok` `warn` `danger` `info`, each with a `-tint` companion
50	(`text-ok` / `bg-ok-tint`). Status colour is never the brand colour.
51	
52	### Radius / elevation / motion
53	
54	`rounded-sm|md|lg|xl|2xl` (8/10/14/20/28px) · `shadow-e1|e2|e3` ·
55	`duration-[var(--t-1)]` 120ms, `--t-2` 200ms, `--t-3` 380ms ·
56	`ease-[var(--ease)]`
57	
58	---
59	
60	## Utility classes
61	
62	`k-focus` — **put this on every interactive element.** One focus ring, product-wide.
63	`k-display` `k-h1` `k-h2` `k-label` — the type scale. `k-label` is the only uppercase.
64	`k-num` — **required** on any figure: credits, prices, counts, dates in a column.
65	`k-scroll-x` — wrap any wide table/code block. The page body must never scroll sideways.
66	`k-msg-in` `k-step-in` `k-step-active` — entrance and progress animations.
67	`k-preview-busy` / `k-preview-idle` — the preview treatment while the AI works.
68	`k-wash` — ambient brand glow inside a hero panel. Sparingly: one per page, at most.
69	`k-gradient-border` — gradient hairline. Reserve for the single most important panel.
70	
71	---
72	
73	## Components (`components/ui/`)
74	
75	Import these. **Do not hand-roll a second version of any of them.**
76	
77	| Component | Notes |
78	| --- | --- |
79	| `Button` `ButtonLink` `IconButton` `buttonClass` | Variants `primary\|secondary\|ghost\|soft\|danger`, sizes `xs\|sm\|md\|lg`. **One `primary` per view.** `IconButton` requires `label`. |
80	| `Card` `CardHeader` `SectionHeader` | `interactive` only if it truly responds. |
81	| `Badge` | `tone` + `dot` + `pulse`. Set `dot` on anything conveying live state — colour alone is not a status channel. |
82	| `Input` `Textarea` `Select` `SearchInput` | Label/hint/error/aria wiring is built in. Never hand-write a bare `<input>`. |
83	| `Progress` `toneForUsage` | Recolours as it fills. `indeterminate` for work with no known end. |
84	| `Skeleton` `SkeletonList` | Stagger with `delay`. |
85	| `EmptyState` | `kind` is required: `empty` (none yet) / `no-results` (filter too narrow) / `unavailable` (does not exist yet). These need different sentences. |
86	| `Menu` | Keyboard + Escape + click-outside already handled. `unavailableReason` greys an item and says why. |
87	| `Modal` `ConfirmModal` | Native `<dialog>`. Confirm buttons are labelled with the verb, never "OK". |
88	| `ToastProvider` `useToast` | Provider is already mounted by `AppShell`. Errors and toasts with an action do not auto-dismiss. |
89	| `Segmented` | Real radios. Used for grid/list and device toggles. |
90	| `AIProgress` `stepsAt` | **The** progress component. See below. |
91	| `Stat` `StatRow` | Any number the customer must understand. |
92	| `Avatar` | Initials only — there is no avatar upload. |
93	| `Spinner` | |
94	
95	## Shell (`components/app/`)
96	
97	`AppShell` wraps every portal page and already provides the sidebar, mobile
98	drawer, bottom bar and toast host. **A page renders content only** — no page
99	supplies its own nav, no page sets a background, no page mounts a second
100	`ToastProvider`.
101	
102	Navigation lives in `components/app/nav.ts`. An item may only be added there
103	once it is backed by real data; `soon: true` marks the ones that are not.
104	
105	---
106	
107	## AI progress is one object, not three spinners
108	
109	`AIProgress` is rendered by the initial build overlay, by the chat panel during
110	an edit, and beside the preview. All three must show the **same steps in the
111	same state**, because the customer reads them as one thing happening.
112	
113	**Drive `state` from real build signals.** A timer that walks the list forward on
114	its own is a fake — and it will still be sitting on "Finalizing" long after a
115	build has failed. The build genuinely does not know its percentage (it is an
116	agent loop of unknown length), which is exactly why this is a named-step list
117	and not a progress bar.
118	
119	---
120	
121	## What does not exist (audited — do not build UI that pretends otherwise)
122	
123	| Thing | Reality |
124	| --- | --- |
125	| **Plans / subscriptions** | None. No plan, price, or renewal date. Checkout is one-off `payment` mode for credit packs. **Never render a "Pro" chip or "$X/month".** |
126	| **Credit reset date** | Credits never expire. There is no monthly allowance and no reset day — the spend cap is a *rolling* 30 days chosen so there is no reset. |
127	| **Invoices / payment method** | Not fetched from Stripe. The credit ledger is the only history. |
128	| **Thumbnails** | Nothing captures a screenshot. No headless browser. |
129	| **Project status** | Only `publishedAt` → Published / Draft. No `archived`. "Building" is derivable from `Build.status = RUNNING` but has no staleness rule, so it is not yet trustworthy. |
130	| **Domains** | No model, no field, no route. Sites live at `<slug>.kodely.site` only. |
131	| **Integrations** | Nothing customer-facing. |
132	| **Support tickets** | No ticket model. `SupportNote` is admin-write-only and explicitly never shown to the customer. |
133	| **Storage / bandwidth** | Not measured anywhere. |
134	| **Workspaces / members / roles** | No concept of it. Ownership is one FK: `Project.userId`. |
135	| **Avatar upload, password change, 2FA, notification prefs** | None. |
136	
137	**Sessions list and revoke, and editing `User.name`, are now BUILT** — see
138	`/settings/security` and `/settings`. Note what `Session` actually records:
139	`id · userId · tokenHash · expiresAt · createdAt`, and nothing else. There is no
140	user agent, no IP, no last-seen and no device. Do not add a column for them
141	casually: `/legal/rights` and the data export both enumerate in writing
142	everything the database holds, so a new personal-data field silently makes two
143	published documents wrong.
144	
145	### The rule
146	
147	A screen that looks operable and is not is worse than an absent one. A screen
148	that says "this does not exist yet, here is what you have instead" is neither.
149	Use `EmptyState kind="unavailable"` and say plainly what is missing.

2	 * The prompt wizard's data model and its one real job: turning a handful of
3	 * answers into a PROMPT.
4	 *
5	 * ## Why this file emits text and not a config object
6	 *
7	 * The wizard's output is a plain-English prompt that lands in a textarea the
8	 * user can read, edit and delete half of. It is never a hidden state blob that
9	 * /api/generate reads. Three reasons, in order of weight:
10	 *
11	 *   1. There is exactly one build path. The raw composer is the default entry
12	 *      point and always will be; if the wizard emitted a config, we would have
13	 *      two paths to test, debug and eval, and the second one would rot.
14	 *   2. The user stays in control. They can see what the wizard decided on their
15	 *      behalf. A config object cannot offer that.
16	 *   3. lib/templates.ts already proves the shape. The 23 starter prompts are
17	 *      exactly what an expert-written wizard output looks like — audience,
18	 *      tone, ordered sections, bracketed placeholders, link-outs instead of
19	 *      forms. So the wizard's job is to help someone produce one of those, not
20	 *      to invent a parallel format.
21	 *
22	 * ## Zero model calls
23	 *
24	 * Everything here is local string work. /api/enhance is auth-gated and rate
25	 * limited per user id, and most people meeting the wizard have no account —
26	 * an affordance that 401s on click is worse than no affordance. So assembly is
27	 * synchronous, offline, and identical signed in or out.
28	 *
29	 * Enhance is deliberately NOT part of the wizard flow afterwards either. The
30	 * wizard's output is already a structured brief in Enhance's own house style
31	 * (Audience / tone / ordered sections / bracketed placeholders), and it is
32	 * routinely longer than lib/enhance.ts's MAX_PROMPT_CHARS — /api/enhance
33	 * answers exactly that case with "That's already detailed enough to build".
34	 * The wizard assembles; Enhance polishes a one-liner. Neither duplicates the
35	 * other, and neither gets to overwrite the palette the user picked.
36	 *
37	 * ## Colour is hexes, never adjectives
38	 *
39	 * "Warm and modern" is the instruction that produces the same three sites every
40	 * time. Every look direction below resolves to a real preset in
41	 * lib/assets/patterns.ts, and the emitted prompt carries that preset's id AND
42	 * its literal stops, plus a pointer at the find_assets tool the builder already
43	 * has. That makes the choice unambiguous for the model and auditable for us.

397	 * the caller can say so instead of navigating into an empty composer.
398	 */

406	    // has no image path of its own yet (the logo / reference-screenshot step is
407	    // deliberately not built), so it always clears this.
408	    sessionStorage.removeItem(PENDING_PROMPT_IMAGE_KEY);
409	    return true;
410	  } catch {
411	    return false;
412	  }
413	}

/**
 * The only place in Kodely that opens a socket to an address a user chose.
 *
 * Not a route — a module colocated with the one route that uses it, so that the
 * network half of the site import stays out of `lib/site-import.ts` (which has
 * to stay importable from a browser bundle) and so that everything with a
 * `node:` import is in one file that can be read top to bottom.
 *
 * ## Read this before changing anything below
 *
 * The process running this code holds DATABASE_URL, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY and
 * ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and it sits inside a private network. An SSRF here is not
 * "an unwanted HTTP request", it is credential disclosure. Every control below
 * is written on the assumption that the caller is trying to reach
 * 169.254.169.254, and several of them exist only because the obvious
 * implementation (`fetch(userUrl)`) is wrong in a way that looks right.
 *
 * ## What is defended, and how
 *
 *  1. SCHEME + PORT + CREDENTIALS + HOSTNAME SHAPE — `validateImportUrl` in
 *     lib/site-import.ts, before anything resolves.
 *
 *  2. DNS IS RESOLVED HERE, EXPLICITLY, and every address that comes back is
 *     classified. Not the hostname — the addresses. A hostname allowlist or
 *     denylist is decoration: `evil.test` is a public name and its A record is
 *     whatever the attacker's zone file says today.
 *
 *  3. EVERY answer must be public, not merely the one we pick. A name that
 *     publishes 93.184.216.34 and 10.0.0.5 together is either broken or an
 *     attack, and picking the good one would mean the same lookup a moment
 *     later could hand a different answer to something else.
 *
 *  4. THE REBIND HOLE IS CLOSED BY PINNING. This is the control most
 *     implementations miss, so it is worth being explicit about the failure it
 *     prevents. The naive shape is:
 *
 *         const ips = await dns.resolve(host);   // 93.184.216.34 — fine
 *         if (ips.every(isPublic)) await fetch(url);   // resolves AGAIN
 *
 *     Two lookups, and the attacker controls the TTL. Set it to 0 and answer
 *     the first query with a public address and the second with 169.254.169.254
 *     and every check passed while the socket went somewhere else. It is not
 *     even a race you have to win reliably — the attacker just retries.
 *
 *     The fix is that THERE IS ONLY ONE LOOKUP. `pinnedLookup` below is handed
 *     to `https.request` as its resolver, and it ignores the hostname entirely
 *     and returns the single address this code already validated. The TCP
 *     connection provably goes to the address that was checked, because no
 *     second resolution exists to disagree with the first. TLS still validates
 *     the certificate against the real hostname (`servername`), and the `Host`
 *     header still carries the real hostname, so virtual hosting works and the
 *     server sees a completely ordinary request.
 *
 *  5. REDIRECTS ARE FOLLOWED BY HAND. `https.request` does not follow them at
 *     all, which is one reason it is used here instead of `fetch` — `fetch`
 *     follows by default, and a permitted host answering
 *     `Location: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` is the single most

 *     `resolveRedirect` (full URL validation) and then through this function
 *     again (fresh DNS, fresh classification, fresh pin). Capped at

 *  6. BOUNDED. A 5s connect timeout, a 10s deadline over the WHOLE operation
 *     including robots.txt and every hop, a body cap enforced byte by byte
 *     while the response streams, and a redirect count. `Content-Length` is
 *     used only as an early reject — never as the thing that stops the read,

Welcome to the Next.js documentation!

## What is Next.js?

Next.js is a React framework for building full-stack web applications. You use React Components to build user interfaces, and Next.js for additional features and optimizations.

It also automatically configures lower-level tools like bundlers and compilers. You can instead focus on building your product and shipping quickly.

Whether you're an individual developer or part of a larger team, Next.js can help you build interactive, dynamic, and fast React applications.

## How to use the docs

The docs are organized into 3 sections:

- [Getting Started](/docs/app/getting-started): Step-by-step tutorials to help you create a new application and learn the core Next.js features.
- [Guides](/docs/app/guides): Tutorials on specific use cases, choose what's relevant to you.
- [API Reference](/docs/app/api-reference): Detailed technical reference for every feature.

Use the sidebar to navigate through the sections, or search (`Ctrl+K` or `Cmd+K`) to quickly find a page.

## App Router and Pages Router

Next.js has two different routers:

- **App Router**: The newer router that supports new React features like Server Components.
- **Pages Router**: The original router, still supported and being improved.

At the top of the sidebar, you'll notice a dropdown menu that allows you to switch between the [App Router](/docs/app) and the [Pages Router](/docs/pages) docs.

### React version handling

The App Router and Pages Router handle React versions differently:

- **App Router**: Uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries) built-in, which include all the stable React 19 changes, as well as newer features being validated in frameworks, prior to a new React release.

- **Pages Router**: Uses the React version installed in your project's `package.json`.

This approach ensures new React features work reliably in the App Router while maintaining backwards compatibility for existing Pages Router applications.

## Pre-requisite knowledge

Our documentation assumes some familiarity with web development. Before getting started, it'll help if you're comfortable with:

- HTML
- CSS
- JavaScript
- React

If you're new to React or need a refresher, we recommend starting with our [React Foundations course](/learn/react-foundations), and the [Next.js Foundations course](/learn/dashboard-app) that has you building an application as you learn.

Build a one-page website for Bloom Pilates — A reformer pilates studio in Denver for people who tried a big-box gym and hated it. We run small classes, six people maximum, and most of our members come from word of mouth.

Audience: someone who has decided to start training and is comparing two or three local studios. They want to know what a class is actually like, what it costs, and whether beginners are welcome. Tone: energetic but grown-up — motivating, not shouty.

Sections in this order:
1. Hero — the studio name, one line on what makes training here different, and a "Book your first class" button.
2. Classes — 3 or 4 class types, each with a short description, difficulty level and duration.
3. Timetable — a simple weekly grid of day / time / class. Make clear in the copy that this is the current timetable and I keep it up to date by hand.
4. Membership — 2 or 3 price options (drop-in, monthly, intro offer) as plain cards with what each includes.
5. A short "new here?" paragraph answering what to bring and how early to arrive.
6. Hours, address, footer.

Class times, prices, the address, the trainers' names and any claims about results must be bracketed placeholders — never invented.

There is no backend: no sign-up form, no payment, no class booking. The CTAs are [link to your booking system], a tel: link and a mailto: link, labelled so it is obvious where they go.

No photography available — use bold type, a high-contrast palette and inline SVG. Responsive to 380px, dark mode included.

Visual direction — I chose this, so build to it rather than picking your own. Where it disagrees with a colour or type hint earlier in this brief, this wins:
- Look: Soft and elegant. Quiet and refined — pale tones, light serif, whitespace doing the work.
- Palette: blush (#FFE4E6 to #FBCFE8, 150deg). Use find_assets with the query "blush" to pull the exact gradient source, make those the dominant colours, and derive the rest of the palette from those hexes. Do not substitute a different colour, and do not fall back to indigo or violet.
- Typography: light serif headings (ui-serif, Georgia, serif) at restrained sizes, with small uppercase labels at wide letter-spacing.
- Density: whitespace-led — very generous margins, smaller type, nothing crowded.

Adjustments that override the visual direction above wherever the two disagree:
- Typography: serif headings from the system serif stack (ui-serif, Georgia, serif) over a plain sans body. Remember there are no web fonts of any kind — the CSP allows none, base64 included.
- Density: roomy. A long vertical rhythm, roughly one idea per screen, generous whitespace, nothing crowded.

Tone of voice for every word on the page — this is the answer to the "Tone:" placeholder above, so resolve it rather than leaving the bracket in: calm and understated — short sentences, no exclamation marks, nothing oversold.

More about this business, in the owner's own words — treat this as the source of truth for what the site is for:
The website needs to make a nervous first-timer feel like they could walk in.

These are the real details for this business. Use them exactly as written — in the copy, in the <title>, in the meta description and in every call to action. Anything NOT in this list is something you do not know: leave it as an obvious bracketed placeholder such as [your address] rather than inventing a plausible-looking value.
- Name, spelled and capitalised exactly like this: Bloom Pilates
- Where it is: Denver, Colorado
- What it offers: Reformer classes; Private sessions; Beginner courses
- Email address for enquiries: hello@bloompilates.com
- Phone number: +1 303 555 0134
- Opening hours: Mon-Fri 6am-8pm · Sat 8am-1pm · Sun closed
- Links to use: https://instagram.com/bloompilates

Include these as well as the sections above. Where one of them covers the same ground as a section already listed, merge the two rather than building the same thing twice:

One correction to the brief above first. It says there is no backend and no form should be built. That is right about every other kind of form and wrong about exactly two, so treat this paragraph as overriding it for those two and for nothing else.

Kodely's platform answers `POST /__forms/<name>` on a published site's OWN origin — proxy.ts routes that host back into the app — stores the submission, and emails it to the site owner. A plain HTML form is a navigation rather than a scripted request, so this needs no `fetch`, does not touch `connect-src 'none'`, and is permitted as written by `form-action 'self'`. A form built to the shape below therefore delivers a real message to a real inbox; it is not a decoration.

Still genuinely impossible, and still refused: bookings with availability, accounts and logins, carts and checkout, anything that has to read data back. Those stay link-outs.

Contact form
Contact form. This one genuinely works, so build it rather than substituting a mailto: link:

Build it exactly like this:
- `<form method="post" action="/__forms/contact">`. A plain HTML form and nothing else: no fetch, no onSubmit handler, no JavaScript at all. The browser navigates, which is what the site's strict CSP allows; a scripted request would be blocked.

- A spam honeypot the platform already checks for: `<input type="text" name="_gotcha" tabIndex={-1} autoComplete="off" aria-hidden="true" />` inside a visually-hidden wrapper, so no sighted or screen-reader user ever meets it.
- The submit button reads "Send message" — never "Submit" or "Send".
- One line of small print under it: messages go to [your email address].
Also keep a mailto: link to [your email address] and a tel: link to [your phone number] close by, so a visitor who would rather not use a form still has a way through.

Opening hours
An opening-hours block: days and times in a real <table> or a two-column definition list, aligned so the times line up, and readable without zooming at 380px. Use [your opening hours] exactly as supplied and leave any day that was not supplied as a bracketed placeholder — never guess a closing time, because an invented one sends a real customer to a locked door.

FAQ
An FAQ of five to eight questions, built as native `<details>`/`<summary>` elements (or a React accordion with correct aria-expanded and aria-controls wiring) so keyboard and screen-reader users get the same behaviour. Write questions this kind of business is genuinely asked, answer them in a real voice, and leave any figure or timescale you cannot know as a bracketed placeholder.

I have attached my logo as the reference image for this build. Use it for the brand's colours, weight and general character, and pull the palette towards it wherever that does not fight the visual direction above. ## Contact forms — offered, with one risk you should know about

Verified end to end: `submitSiteForm` stores the row, emails the owner, and `app/projects/[id]/submissions` exists to read them. Draft previews genuinely don't send (`submitSiteForm` refuses any project without `publishedAt`, and the preview route is a different handler) — that caveat sits next to the toggle *and* is re-listed on the review stage.

**The risk:** nothing has ever told the builder that `/__forms/` exists. `lib/agent.ts`'s SYSTEM prompt says "Do not build a contact form", and **all 23 templates plus the generic skeleton repeat it**. My fragment would otherwise be one instruction against twenty-five. So `featuresFragment()` emits an explicit supersession paragraph *before* the fragments (gated on a `supersedesNoFormRule` flag, set on exactly two features), which names the rule it overrides, gives the mechanism, and narrows the override so booking/checkout/login stay refused. The fragment also demands a mailto: and tel: link beside the form, so the contact route works even if the model declines the form.

**Recommendation for whoever owns `lib/agent.ts`:** add the `/__forms/<name>` markup contract to SYSTEM. Until then this override is prompt-level persuasion rather than a guarantee.
